text: Farm animals now live a farmer's day by local sun time: penned at night, driven out to pasture at first light, grazing hardest in the early morning and before dusk, resting and chewing the cud at midday, then brought home. Chickens roost at dusk. After 1920 most cars park overnight and crawl at morning and evening rush hours. Tap one to see what it is doing.

Dinosaur-era map redrawn from a published reconstruction: continents sit where the PALEOMAP PaleoDEMs (Scotese & Wright 2018) put them 70 million years ago. India is now an island far south in the Indian Ocean, Australia and Africa moved to their real places, and the round hole in West Africa is gone.

102 more real inventions and things people made appear where and when they did, from Skara Brae and the Terracotta Army to Hoover Dam, the Manchester Baby, Mosaic and Chandrayaan-3, each a new card; 16 older milestones gain their real place and source.

The asteroid now arrives at its true speed: in the last real second before impact the clock pauses and its final 5 minutes play in real time, 20 km every second, from the northeast at about 60 degrees, with a live distance readout.
Northern and southern lights every night: glowing ovals around the magnetic poles that brighten, widen and turn red in storms, following the real sunspot cycle (SILSO). Tap the label to learn why.

A real Moon (NASA's LRO map, near side always facing us, Apollo 11 at its real spot), a Sun with limb darkening and sunspots that follow the solar cycle, 166 total lunar eclipses from 1901 to 2100 (NASA), five record solar flares, and a 'from the ground' view during eclipses.

Storm paths like the weather channel: the track coloured by strength, the National Hurricane Center's cone of uncertainty, and forecast dots with days and times. Storms now grow and weaken through their lives.
Follow any animal from its card; a strip shows who you're following with a Stop button.
Search: type any animal, plant, place or event (try "velociraptor") from Explore and it flies you there. Things from another era are marked so you know they aren't alive right now.
My home: pin the place you live from Explore and watch it change over time. The pin follows the drifting continents, and the panel lists what happened near it.
Chat now sits on the bottom bar with a dot for new messages. Cards moved into More.

79 more prehistoric animals at their real fossil sites: Ice Age kangaroos, giant mound-builder birds and land crocodiles in Australia, glyptodonts, ground sloths and sparassodonts in South America, giant pigs, buffalo and early elephants in Africa, gomphotheres and early giraffes across Asia, and early sea cows (Paleobiology Database).

Tar pits: at Rancho La Brea and four other real asphalt seeps, animals that wander onto the hidden asphalt get stuck, struggle and slowly sink, and the predators that come for them can get stuck too. Plus 194 more real species interactions, from La Brea sabre-tooths and dire wolves to Arctic tyrannosaurs and Yellowstone wolves.
Realism fixes: Hipparion horses now start 11.4 million years ago, not 23, and Placerias lives only in North America (its only known fossil region).

A cleaner screen: one bottom bar (Explore, Time, Follow, Cards, More) replaces the two rows of buttons, a small Live pill shows who is watching, and the zoom buttons are gone on phones (pinch to zoom). Everything is still there: Explore holds Happening now, Places, the guided tour and Events; More holds Chat, Ideas, name tags, clouds, sound, saved spots and Settings. New preview picture when the site is shared.

A new opening: once per visit, a tiny crew from the current era (raptors in the dinosaur age, then early mammals, cave people, farmers, factory workers or hard-hat builders) carries the screen's bars into place, waves and heads off. Tap to skip; it never plays with reduced motion on. New app icon for the home screen.

The dinosaur-era globe now wears real satellite colours. Every forest, dry woodland and desert of 71 million years ago is painted with real NASA Blue Marble texture taken from a living place of the same kind (the Amazon and Congo for rainforest, Europe and the Appalachians for broadleaf woods, Quebec and Karelia for northern forest, the cerrado and Sahel for dry woodland, the Sahara and Arabia for desert), with natural, wandering edges between them. Exposed Ice Age shelves get the same treatment.

Prehistoric animals now live where their fossils were really found: 1,921 dated fossil sites from the Paleobiology Database for 527 extinct animals, from the last dinosaurs to Ice Age sabre-tooth cats.

Herds and predators now spread across the land instead of crowding into one spot. Each herd has its own home range and walks a daily route on real local time: out to feed at first light, to water, a slow midday, an afternoon feeding ground, then a place to rest for the night. Predators patrol their ranges and Ice Age and modern predators rest by day. Distances come from GPS-collar studies of elephants and lions. Tapping an animal shows where it is on its route, and how far it has walked today. Cars no longer show a diet, people show as omnivores, and double-tapping the play buttons no longer zooms the page.

Lakes and rivers are respected on the ground: in the wild, trees no longer grow in water and land animals start on dry land and walk around it. Today's lakes are no longer painted into older eras (Lake Victoria was dry at the last glacial maximum).

Play as an animal: tap a wild animal and choose "Play as this animal" to walk, run, graze or hunt as it, with a hunger bar. Other animals react to you by the same researched rules, so predators may come for you.

Animals now say what they actually eat: predators list the real prey and carcasses they fed on, with the research it comes from (for example T. rex: Edmontosaurus, Triceratops). Plant diets are being researched next.
Cleaner map: zoomed out you see only continents and oceans; country names appear as you zoom in and never pile up; cities appear when you get close, like Google Earth.

The Ice Age planet now uses real satellite colour and texture (NASA Blue Marble) wherever the land looked as it does today, from 3 million years ago on, fading as the ice sheets grow. Ice sheets, the dry land of Doggerland, Beringia and Sundaland, and the green Sahara keep their reconstructed colours, and there is no longer a jump in 4000 BC.

99 more real inventions and things people made, at their real places and dates: Africa's Ishango bone and Great Zimbabwe, Baghdad's paper mills and al-Khwarizmi's algebra, India's Iron Pillar and Gwalior zero, Korea's Jikji, the Olmec heads, Colossus and M-Pesa. New prehistoric species now appear rare and local and spread over time.
Behind the scenes: the owner can now preview any era on their own device to check how it looks, without touching the shared live world. Visiting any era for everyone opens after the first live run.

Realism fixes: oaks and maples no longer grow in the dinosaur age (oaks first appear about 56 million years ago, maples about 61), and the South American sabre-tooth Smilodon populator, the giant sloth Lestodon and the short-faced bear Arctotherium now die out at the end of the Ice Age instead of living on to today.

394 more real animal interactions (1,554 in all): leopards stalking peafowl, alpacas chasing foxes from the flock, killer whales chasing blue whales, wildebeest and crocodiles at the Mara crossing, giant hyenas stealing sabre-cat kills, Dinofelis hunting giant geladas, crocodiles crushing turtles in the last dinosaur age, duckbill herds, and tyrannosaurs chasing oviraptorosaurs. Tap an animal to see what it is doing.

Cards now come as half a card. To finish one, find the real thing in the world (tap the animal, or open the event or place), then answer up to three questions about it. Every question is built from the card's own sourced facts, and wrong options are real look-alikes, like animals from other ages or fossil sites on other continents. Finished cards get a gold border. Cards from eras that have already ended, and plants, go straight to the questions.

The planet looks far more real: from 4,000 years ago on, Earth uses NASA's Blue Marble satellite colors (public domain); the atmosphere glows blue on the day side and orange at sunset; a thin haze softens the horizon when zoomed out; oceans catch a sun glint; clouds follow real belts like the equator's storms and the stormy southern latitudes; and ancient coastlines are softer and more natural.

69 famous shipwrecks, from the Bronze Age Uluburun trader and the Antikythera wreck to the Mary Rose, Vasa, Titanic, Lusitania, Endurance and Estonia, now lie at their real sites. Each sinks on its real date (great losses of life are remembered quietly), shows as a dot on the sea when you zoom in, and a sonar ring marks the day a lost wreck was found or raised. Tap a dot for what happened, lives lost, depth and sources.

Dinosaur-era map: no Hudson Bay, Great Lakes or Baltic before the ice ages carved them, no Red Sea before it opened, and the Western Interior Seaway now runs from the Gulf of Mexico to Canada at its real width.

Skylines rise on their real dates: 1,488 real skyscrapers, towers and masts 100 m or taller from Wikidata stand at their true places and heights (drawn 10× taller so you can see them from the air), grow during their last year of building and vanish when pulled down. Tap one for its height, floors and opening year; every one 300 m or taller gets its own moment on the timeline.

Animals move like animals: legs swing in a walking rhythm while they travel (faster when they run, still when they rest), bigger animals step more slowly, tails sway, pterosaurs and plesiosaurs flap, fish swim with side-to-side strokes, and animals are darker on the back and paler underneath. Mammals have a new shape with a real neck, head and tail instead of a box.

Ice-age ice sheets now follow a real reconstruction of the last deglaciation (ICE-NADI-1 and ICE-7G, every 500 years): the Laurentide, Cordilleran, Scandinavian and British ice sheets cover their real areas, Hudson Bay and the Barents Sea fill with ice, and they melt back on their real dates. Rivers and lakes under the ice are hidden.

64 more real prehistoric animals and 27 fossil trees, each placed only where its fossils were found: early whales and hoofed mammals of Eocene India, marsupials and penguins of forested Antarctica, Africa's giant hyaenodonts and dagger-toothed cats, Australia's Riversleigha snake and killer kangaroo, the Arctic tyrannosaur Nanuqsaurus, the 17.5 m Pyrenean titanosaur Abditosaurus, the last pterosaurs of Morocco and Jordan, Sicily's 90 cm dwarf elephant and the Channel Islands pygmy mammoth. New trees include hemlock, cedar, hornbeam, linden, Banksia and date palm. They all become trading cards.
Velociraptor now has a detailed, feathered body built from fossil anatomy, and it walks, runs, swishes its tail and breathes.
Nights on the ground are no longer pitch black: dim blue starlight keeps the land, trees and animals faintly visible, and it gets brighter when the Moon is up and near full.

Ocean ships move at their era's real speeds: sailing ships at about 4 to 6 knots, steamers at about 9, container ships at 22 knots and, since 2008, slow steaming at about 18. Ships slow into harbour and wait in port (about 12 days under sail, about a day today), steam gradually replaces sail from the 1840s to the 1930s, and tapping a ship tells you what it is, its speed, its route and which day of the voyage it's on.

486 more real animal interactions, most of them for the last dinosaurs and sea reptiles 72 to 66 million years ago (a young Gorgosaurus that ate small dinosaurs, Tylosaurus with a plesiosaur in its gut, ankylosaurs clubbing each other). New: predators steal kills, so hyenas and lions take each other's meals and bears take over wolf and cougar kills.
